new_statements.quote: [T6.1, p. 135:] Acute accent | Ngarámata | younger brother | b:20:10.1 | shows stress on second syllable | hundreds [p. 226:] Of over fifty examples of the imperative in the Dawes/Anon data, almost all end in a; and, where stress is indicated, it falls on the final syllable. [p. 265:] -bi-ra-ng and -bi-la-ng are based on the stem-forming suffix -bi (see T8.1 and §8.4.2.3 and throughout Chapter 8), on which the stress falls (as noted by Dawes, and shown here in bold type), making them structurally distinct from -gulang.
new_statements.citation: Steele, Jeremy Macdonald. 2005. The aboriginal language of Sydney: a partial reconstruction of the indigenous language of Sydney based on the notebooks of William Dawes of 1790-91, informed by other records of the Sydney and surrounding languages to c.1905. MA (Hons) thesis, Macquarie University.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (356 pp, text layer) with extracted text at the stated PDF pages. All three quoted passages are there verbatim: PDF p. 157 (printed 135) §6.2 'Macrons, breves and diacritics', Table T6.1 row 'Acute accent | Ngarámata | younger brother | b:20:10.1 | shows stress on second syllable | hundreds'; PDF p. 248 (printed 226) §8.7 Imperative: 'Of over fifty examples of the imperative in the Dawes/Anon data, almost all end in a; and, where stress is indicated, it falls on the final syllable.' followed by 'the imperative a, which generally takes the stress, as indicated by Dawes using an acute accent [á]' and, on printed p. 227, 'In X8.73, the stress is not shown to fall on the imperative suffi…
new_statements.rule_in_words: No source states a general word-stress rule. The language is known only from 1790s and c.1900 manuscripts. Steele reads Dawes' acute accent (hundreds of tokens, one per word) as a stress mark; his table glosses it with a second-syllable example (Nga-RA-ma-ta), while imperative forms in -a/-la carry stress on the final suffix and the stem-forming suffix -bi is stressed in -birang/-bilang. Troy 1994 (p. 25) says only that Dawes 'only ever accented one syllable of a word' and that the acute probably indicates stress. Net: stress apparently mobile and morphologically conditioned, position unresolved.
new_statements.exceptions: Steele p. 227: in X8.73 Eereéra 'throw!' the stress is not on the imperative suffix; p. 176 n. 2: wára wará 'just now' vs wará wará 'go away!' differ by 'stressing', recorded three times by Dawes.
new_statements.domain_note: All observations come from an 18th-century English officer's acute-accent marks on single words and short sentences (Dawes' notebooks a, b); Troy states phonological analysis is impossible without spoken data and her sound system is hypothetical. Word-level marks; no phrase-level analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog sydn1236 'Sydney' (ISO xdk) covers the coastal Iyora/Eora (Port Jackson, Dawes' data 1790-91) and inland Dharug/Dharruk (Mathews 1901, c.1900) varieties; Troy 1994 treats them as coastal and inland dialects of one 'Sydney Language', Steele 2005 names the language Biyal-Biyal and reconstructs it mainly from Dawes' coastal material. All stress observations above derive from Dawes' coastal notebooks.

sources.note: Ch. 6 Phonology (pp. 131-161) has no stress subsection. Table T6.1 (p. 135) glosses Dawes' acute accent as 'shows stress on second syllable' for the example Ngarámata 'younger brother', frequency 'hundreds'; p. 226 (§8.7): imperatives 'almost all end in a; and, where stress is indicated, it falls on the final syllable'; p. 265: stem-forming suffix -bi in -birang/-bilang is the syllable 'on which the stress falls (as noted by Dawes)'; p. 176 n.2: wára wará 'just now' vs wará wará 'go away!' differ by stressing. No general word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Troy, Jakelin. 1994. The Sydney Language. Canberra: the author (with the Australian Dictionaries Project and AIATSIS). 117 pp. [cited by Steele as Troy 1993-94]
sources.note: 'The sound system' (pp. 22-27) is explicitly a hypothetical inventory built from orthography; the only stress remark is p. 25: 'Dawes used accute accents over all the vowels and the semi-vowel y, but only ever accented one syllable of a word. His usage suggests that he used accute to indicate stress.' No statement of where stress falls.
